Multiple methods and formulas have been proposed with some limitations due to variation in breed and size (especially in dogs), litter size (only for cats), gestational period in which the measurement is performed, and measuring technique. 20 26 28 These formulas allow to calculate the DBP. In small- and medium-sized dogs, the internal diameter of the chorionic cavity (ICC) measured in the ﬁ rst half of pregnancy and the transverse biparietal skull diameter (BD) in the second half seem to be the most useful parameters, with 85% to 95% of reported accuracy in predicting DBP with an error of 1 2 days. Accuracy is higher at week 5 of gestation and decreases after week 8. In large and giant dogs, the reported accuracy of measuring ICC is greater compared to the BD. 27 Table 44.4 summarizes reported formulas that can be used in dogs and cats to calculate the number of DBP. Establishing litter size by ultrasound is more challenging compared to radiography; this is due to technical dif ﬁ culties (amount of fecal and intestinal gas content, overlapping of fe- tuses), limited ﬁ eld of view, and operator experience. 29 Em- bryonic or fetal resorption has an estimated incidence between 5% and 13% in bitches; this is a potential cause of litter over- estimation. Reported accuracy of ultrasonography in deter- mining litter size is 65%, inc reas in g to 89.5 % if an er ror of 1 is co nsi de re d. 29 To in cre ase th e suc ces s of the eva lu ati on, sc ann ing in tr an sve rse pl ane fro m ca uda l to cr ani al fo llow ing the tw o ut er ine hor ns at aro und 30 day s of ge sta tio n is rec omme nde d. 7 ABNOR MAL RADIOG RAPHIC AND ULTRAS ONOGRA PHIC FINDIN GS DU RING PREGN ANCY Combining ultrasound and radiology can be useful to detect uterine or fetal abnormalities during pregnancy. 30 31 Early resorption of underdeveloped or malformed em- bryos can be documented ultrasonographically, the features depending upon the timing of the resorption. Early during pregnancy, a characteristic appearance of echogenic particles within the yolk sac, progressive loss of ﬂ uid volume, and hypoechogenicity of the adjacent uterus are observed. Gesta- tional sacs are more irregular in shape and smaller compared to normal ones ( Fig. 44.7A ). Later cases are characterized by loss of the fetal heartbeat and fetal movements, blurring of the fetal margins, and more echogenic allantoic ﬂ uid. 31 Accumulation of gas in the fetal stomach or in the uterus can also be observed. Some fetal malformations can be diagnosed during pregnancy, for example, hydrocephalus and hydrops fetalis, where subcu- taneous thickening due to edema, pleural, and pericardial ﬂ uid is reported. 30 Radiographic signs of fetal death may be observed approx- imately 24 hours after death and are less reliable than sono- graphic indicators. The presence of gas within or around the fetus, overlapping or misalignment of the bones of the cranium, a tightly curled fetus, and collapse of the fetal skeleton may be evident ( Fig. 44.8A,B ). Care must be taken to differentiate these ﬁ ndings from gastrointestinal gas and projection obliquity especially in early phases. The presence of delayed develop- ment of a fetus relative to litter mates is also an indication of demise ( Fig. 44.9A ). After 14 days, the uterus diameter is less than 1 cm and distinct uterine layering is not visible by ultrasound. 34 ABNOR MAL RADIOG RAPH IC AND ULTRA SONOGRA PHIC FINDIN GS IN OVA RIAN DISE ASES Ovarian Remnant Syndrome This results from hormone production by ovarian remnant tis- sue, usually secondary to incomplete surgery. The right ovary is more frequently involved. Presurgical ultrasound is effective to identify the residual ovary especially during estrus; however, false-negative or false-positive studies are possible. The remnant presents as a hypoechoic structure often with cystic compo- nent located caudal to one of the kidneys. 35 Ovarian Cysts Functional (follicular or luteal) and nonfunctional ovarian cysts occur as solitary or multiple ﬂ uid- ﬁ lled structures of variable size that are unilateral or bilateral in the bitch. 36 Larger cysts can be recognized radiographically and should be considered as a differential diagnosis for ovarian masses ( Fig. 44.11A ). 3 Ultrasonographically, regardless of their origin, they appear as anechoic, well-de ﬁ ned structures with thin wall and distal acoustic enhancement that may deform the outer margin of the ovary (see Fig. 44.11B ). The size of the cyst does not correlate with the hormonal production, and follicular and luteal cysts often coexist in the same ovary. 36 Ovarian cysts may not be distinguishable from normal folliculi or corpora lutea during estrus; however, if the diameter is larger than 1 cm, a cyst is suspected. Correlation with clinical data (prolonged heat or anestrus, persistent diestrus, signs of hyperestrogenism) and hormonal status (increased estradiol or progesterone level) is needed to differentiate the two situations. Alternatively, ultra- sound can be used to monitor the cystic structure over time. Normal follicles and corpora lutea should not persist longer than 30 and 60 days, respectively. Functional ovarian cysts predispose the bitch to the development of cystic endometrial hyperplasia (CEH) pyometra complex. Uterine stump disease may occur after ovariohyster- ectomy due to early postsurgical bleeding or late infection/ granulomatous in ﬂ ammation of the caudal uterine stump. Stump pyometra is associated with residual functional ovarian tissue. Abscesses or granulomas can develop as reaction to surgical material, whereas severe bleeding may be secondary to coagulopathy. In radiographs, a focal area of increased radio- pacity may be observed between the colon and urinary bladder in the lateral view. This cannot be differentiated from neoplasia arising from the uterine stump. With ultrasound, thickening of the uterine stump of variable echogenicity is observed, often with a complex mass appearance. 7 One or multiple pockets of echogenic ﬂ uid may be present in case of recent bleeding or pus accumulation. Sometimes, surgical material in the granu- loma can be present as hyperechoic foci associated with shadowing. Complications in case of site infection include involvement of adjacent bladder neck or vesico-urethral junc- tion and peritonitis with ﬁ stulous tracts. Rarely, plant foreign bodies may migrate from the vagina to the uterine body and horns. They usually appear as linear, hyperechoic, spindle-shaped structures of variable length, possibly associated with shadowing ( Fig. 44.19 eFig. 44.8 ). Fluid accumulation, thickening of the uterine wall, and changes of the surrounding peritoneum can be observed. Uterine Neoplastic and Nonneoplastic Nodules and Masses Uterine neoplasia is considered rare in small animals, usually occurring in middle-aged to older animals; however, uterine adenocarcinoma has been reported in dogs and cats younger than 1 year of age. Leiomyoma is the most common tumor in dogs; this is a benign, slow-growing, noninvasive, and non- metastasizing neoplasia, often incidentally diagnosed. Malignant aggressive adenocarcinoma is more frequently observed in cats. Other types of benign and malignant neoplasia can be rarely found in both species. 37 Uterine nonneoplastic nodules and masses include granu- lomas, polyps, and focal or multifocal uterine wall hyperplasia. Polyps are focal growths of the uterine wall projecting into the lumen. They are variable in number and size, pedunculated or sessile, often associated with luminal ﬂ uid accumulation and rarely with torsion. 44 Masses arising from the uterus can be identi ﬁ ed radio- graphically depending on their size; however, even if large, they cannot be distinguished from segmental ﬂ uid. They pre- sent as soft tissue opacity, rarely mineralized. They are located in the midventral abdomen if originating from the uterine horns or in a more caudal position, between the colon and urinary bladder, if growing from the uterine body or cervix. 3 46 Dorsal displacement of the descending colon and cranial compression of the urinary bladder can be observed with large caudal masses. Differential diagnoses include extrauterine masses arising from the vagina, ovary, or mesentery. Identifying vascular supply from an ovarian, uterine, or vaginal vessel can be used to con ﬁ rm the genital origin of the mass. 51 For this reason, dual-phase CT scan, acquiring arterial and venous phases separately, can be useful (see Fig. 44.12 ). Placing a urinary catheter can be useful in case of large masses to assess the position and involvement of the urethra. 52 The enhancement evaluated in the postcontrast series provides information about the vascularization of the lesion. Ultrasound on the other hand provides detailed information about the abnormalities of the testicular parenchyma and of the adnexa (scrotum, epididymis, distal part of the spermatic cord with the ductus deferens, vessels, and nerves). 54 Due to their super ﬁ cial location, scrotal or inguinal testicles are best imaged with a high-frequency (8 13 MHz) linear probe. Longitudinal and transverse views of both testes are acquired and compared. Color, power, and pulsed-wave Doppler can be used to assess the arterial and venous ﬂ ow and to investigate parenchymal vascularization. 55 56 For the search of retained abdominal testicles, which are more deeply located, a convex probe with mid to high frequency is often necessary especially in large dogs. Hydrocele is the most common cause of extratesticular ﬂ uid collection, and can result from trauma, neoplasia, infarction, torsion, or infection or can be idiopathic. Hydrocele may also develop secondary to peritoneal effusion, when ﬂ uid passes through the inguinal canal, and this may be associated with jejunal herniation. Hematoceles may occur with trauma, neoplasia, or diabetes mellitus. Pyoceles result from abscess rupture often within a pre-existing hydrocele. Extratesticular ﬂ uid collection is easily visualized as an anechoic to echogenic band surrounding the testicle, depending on the cellular con- tent. Other indications for ultrasound include tunica vaginalis diseases like malformations, infections, trauma, or neoplasia. However, in puppies and kittens until 6 months of age, the small and soft testes can move from the scrotum to the inguinal canal. In dogs, a genetic basis is suspected, with a reported incidence range from 1% to 15%, higher in small-size breed, most frequently unilateral and right sided. 68 Feline cryptorchidism is less frequent compared to dogs. Ultrasound has a high predictive value for the ﬁ nal, surgical location of a retained testicle. 69 The ultrasonographic search of the cryptorchid testicle is best performed with the animal in dorsal recumbency. First, the affected side is identi ﬁ ed by palpation of the scrotal testicle; this restricts the search to 50%. The scan starts in the subcutaneous inguinal region from the scrotum to the inguinal ring, then it continues in the abdomen just lateral to the urinary bladder neck cranially to the caudal pole of the ipsilateral kidney ( Fig. 44.25 ). The testicle must be differentiated from the inguinal or colic/jejunal lymph nodes based on the shape (oval for the testicle and more elongated for the lymph nodes), the absence of the hilus, and the presence of the testicle mediastinum. The retained testicle is usually smaller compared to the scrotal one but similar in echogenicity and structure. Even subtle changes in echogenicity or structure should be considered suspect for neoplastic transformation. Testicle agenesis is rare however possible. If a suspected testi- cle is not identi ﬁ ed, CT or MRI can be useful as further diag- nostic methods. Neoplasia Canine testicular neoplasia is common in old intact dogs, with a reported prevalence between 9% and 27%, and is mainly rep- resented by three types of tumors: interstitial cell (Leydig cell), Sertoli cell, and seminomas. Up to 20% of dogs diagnosed with testicular cancer have more than one primary testicular tumor; most of them are characterized by local invasion but rarely metastasize, with the highest metastatic rate (less than 15%) reported for Sertoli cell tumors and seminomas. 37 The risk of developing testicular neoplasia increases with a retained testis. Hyperestrogenism and femininization syndrome are commonly associated with Sertoli cell tumors. The main clinical signs include bilateral symmetric alopecia and hyperpigmentation, pendulous prepuce, gynecomastia, galactorrhea, atrophy of the penis, and squamous metaplasia of the prostate. Severe pancy- topenia can also develop. Independent of the tumor type, at- rophy of the contralateral testicle is common. As in ovarian neoplasia, the mass can be located between the caudal pole of the kidney and the inguinal canal. With large or mineralized masses, abdominal radiographs can show the lesion located in the mid to caudoventral abdomen ( Fig. 44.26 eFigs. 44.12 and 44.13 ). If caudally located, the enlarged testicle can be confused with the urinary bladder or with a large para-prostatic cyst. 1157: Susanne M. Stieger-Vanegas D iagnostic imaging is an important component in the clinical evaluation of animals with gastrointestinal disease. Survey radiographs are usually the ﬁ rst im- aging modality, often followed or sometimes replaced by an ultrasound examination. Contrast radiographic studies remain in use but they are laborious and time consuming and are often replaced by ultrasound. Nevertheless, contrast radiography re- mains important for evaluation of functional disorders of the stomach and obstructive processes. Computed tomography (CT) is used increasingly for evaluation of the gastrointestinal tract, especially when disease staging is required. While mag- netic resonance (MR) imaging is regularly used in human pa- tients, it is rarely used for the evaluation of the gastrointestinal tract in animals. The greater omentum, which is a large, lacy, fat-containing double folded structure, attaches to the stomach and extends caudally to the urinary bladder, covering the intestines ventrally and laterally. The super ﬁ cial aspect of the greater omentum originates from the greater curvature of the stomach and con- tinues to the proximal part of the duodenum in alignment with the attachment of the lesser omentum to the duodenum. 1 3 The gastrosplenic ligament is part of the greater omentum and connects the hilus of the spleen to the greater curvature of the fundus and body of the stomach. 1 The lesser omentum is small and extends from the liver to lesser curvature of the stomach and the cranial part of the duodenum. 1 3 The largest aspect of the lesser omentum is the hepatogastric ligament connecting the liver with the lesser curvature of the stomach. 1 IMAG ING PROC EDUR ES Radiography Indications Radiography is used commonly to evaluate the stomach. Gastric dilation and volvulus (GDV), a frequently occurring life- threatening disease in dogs, can usually be diagnosed radio- graphically. Furthermore, mineral or metal attenuating foreign bodies are easily detected on survey radiographs. Additionally, survey radiographs are highly sensitive for evaluating the presence of peritoneal gas, if a gastric perforation is suspected. Survey radiographs are also an important baseline if a contrast radiographic study is planned. Radiographic Technique Three, or preferably four, views of the abdomen are required for a thorough evaluation. 4 Performing left lateral, right lateral, ventrodorsal (VD), and dorsoventral (DV) views of the abdomen is especially valuable for the evaluation of the stom- ach as the position of the patient affects the position of the luminal gas and ﬂ uid within the stomach. 5 Due to gravity, ﬂ uid settles dependently, and gas rises to the highest part of the lumen of the stomach. This was discussed in detail in Chapter 38 . These changes in appearance of the stomach help to eval- uate all aspects of the stomach. Oblique views may occasionally be of value to isolate or project certain areas of the stomach, such as the pylorus, especially when a foreign body or pyloric wall mass is suspected. Radiographic examination of the stomach in an animal that has fasted for 12 to 24 hours may be more informative than when the stomach is in the ambient state, as ingesta within the stomach may obscure some lesions or simulate other lesions. 6 8 However, this is not done routinely due to time constraints, and in some patients fasting may be contraindicated. Also, many drugs used for treatment of gastrointestinal disorders or for sedation to facilitate radiographic positioning, alter gastric motility and may cause gas distention of the stomach. Normal Radiographic Findings The stomach is usually easily recognized by its location, shape, and the content of gas, ingesta, or both. The entire stomach may not be discernible on survey radiographs if it is empty or if gastric ﬂ uid silhouettes with the liver or other abdominal structures. As a general guide, the axis of the stomach from the fundus through the body and pylorus on the lateral view is either perpendicular to the spine, parallel to the ribs, or somewhere between these angles ( Figs. 45.2A,B and 45.3A ). In VD radiographs, the long axis of the stomach is generally perpendicular to the spine with the stomach running transversely across the abdomen, making the angular notch dif ﬁ cult to identify (see Fig. 45.2C ). On the VD view of the dog, the cardia, fundus, and body of the stomach are located to the left of midline, and the pyloric portions are located to the right of midline ( Fig. 45.4A ). The pyloric sphincter in the dog usually is located in the right cra- nial abdominal quadrant at approximately the level of the 10th or 11th rib and is usually cranial to the pyloric canal. 9 In immature dogs the pylorus may be located closer to midline than in adults. 10 Variations in the appearance of the stomach in the dog based on breed conformation have been described. 9 On the VD view of the cat, the stomach is more acutely angled compared to the dog, with the pylorus located at or near the midline (see Figs. 45.3B and 45.4B ). A gas pocket may be trapped occasionally in the fundus in a left lateral view. ABNOR MAL GASTR IC CONTEN T Gastric Foreign Bodies Radiopaque material within the stomach is commonly identi- ﬁ ed on survey radiographs ( Fig. 45.26 eFig. 45.10 ). These opacities are most often the result of ingested food or bone fragments and may have no clinical signi ﬁ cance if they are small and cause no obstructive pattern. More clinically signi ﬁ cant foreign bodies, such as ﬁ shhooks and needles, are also readily visible and present no diagnostic dilemma. The ﬁ nding of discoid metallic foreign bodies is signi ﬁ cant, because certain zinc-containing coins (U.S. pennies minted after 1982 and Euro cents) can induce intravascular hemolysis and hemolytic anemia. 102 104 Radiographs of the abdomen are indicated in the evaluation of patients with intravascular hemolysis for this reason. Other types of metallic objects may also contain zinc. Determining the denomination of suspected coins may be possible radiographically ( eFig. 45.11 ). If projected en face, the diameter can be measured and corrected for magni ﬁ cation and compared to the known diameter of coins. Early surgical intervention might help to alleviate the risk of gastric perforation or obstruction secondary to ingested mag- nets. 105 106 It is important to remember that certain metallic foreign bodies are not metal attenuating on radiographs; for example, aluminum is relatively radiolucent and is therefore dif ﬁ cult to detect on survey radiographs. It is also important to remember that dogs may swallow glue containing diphenyl- methane diisocyanate, which expands extensively when exposed to moisture in the stomach ﬁ lling the gastric lumen and thereby resulting in a severe out ﬂ ow obstruction ( eFig. 45.12 ). 107 The stomach may occasionally contain nondescript radi- opaque material of questionable signi ﬁ cance ( Fig. 45.27 ). The persistence of the abnormality is important. If the patient is stable and endoscopy is not used, repeat radiographs made af- ter fasting for 12 to 24 hours may provide valuable information about the digestibility or potential transit of the suspicious material. A greater problem exists with radiographic detection of nonopaque gastric foreign bodies. Such objects are usually dif ﬁ cult to see on survey radiographs. Several approaches exist to help in the radiographic identi ﬁ cation of nonopaque gastric foreign bodies. The simplest is to use different patient positions. If the foreign body does not shift dependently with gastric ﬂ uid, then a different view may help outline the foreign body with gas. If a foreign body ingestion is suspected and endoscopy is not available, a contrast radiographic study, ultrasound, or CT study of the abdomen may be necessary for diagnosis. Giving a small amount of barium or gas ( Fig. 45.28 ) may make such foreign bodies easier to see than with a standard gastrogram using a large volume of barium because the large volume may obscure the foreign body. Pneumogastrography is simple, easy to perform, cheap, and quick and requires no special equip- ment and can help outline gastric foreign bodies. 21 The appearance of a foreign body on a gastrogram varies depending on the type of foreign body present. An object such as a solid ball creates a round, discrete ﬁ lling defect within the barium. If the object has a nonabsorbent surface, it may not be visible after the stomach has emptied. Conversely, a rag or sock may not create an initial ﬁ lling defect because the contrast medium may permeate the object. Because of absorption and retention of contrast medium, however, the foreign body may be better visible after the stomach has emptied. Gas containing radiolucent foreign bodies may be dif ﬁ cult to identify. Noticing a focal radiolucency with a consistent shape and often a thin peripheral soft tissue opaque rim is important to identify these foreign bodies ( eFig. 45.13 ). The major radiographic feature of gastric neoplasia is that of a mass lesion that projects into the gastric lumen, creating a ﬁ lling defect within the contrast medium. The more nodular and pedunculated the lesion, the easier it is to recognize it as a distinct mass (see Fig. 45.31 ). Larger masses may also lead to out ﬂ ow obstruction. 139 Smaller mass lesions may be obscured completely by a relatively large volume of barium. Oblique projections, the conformation of the stomach, and peristaltic contractions may all contribute to obscuring some mass lesions of the stomach. Tumors that are diffuse are more dif ﬁ cult to identify. Diffuse in ﬁ ltrative lesions of the stomach wall may not produce distinct ﬁ lling defects. Instead, they may alter the shape of the stomach and produce decreased motility of the involved area. If such diffuse lesions encircle a portion of the stomach, the radio- graphic appearance may be that of an annular narrowing or one in which the stomach has decreased distensibility in the affected area (see Fig. 45.31B eFig. 45.14 ). Because of varia- tions in appearance of the stomach created by peristalsis, persistence of a suspected abnormality on sequential radio- graphs is important. As stated earlier, the recognition of a gastric ulcer should also suggest the possibility of gastric neoplasia. Gastric masses can be found on ultrasound examination of the stomach, thus often eliminating the need for radiographic contrast studies. Acute gastritis may result from a variety of causes and is rarely associated with radio- graphic abnormalities. One of the forms of acute gastritis called exercise-induced gastritis is an important condition to remember as it is associated with a high morbidity and mor- tality in working dogs and sled dogs. 117 Chronic gastritis is diagnosed infrequently clinically and may also result from a variety of causes. All animals reported to have emphysematous gastritis had severe clinical signs including anorexia, hema- temesis, lethargy, and leukocytosis and all animals had a poor outcome and were euthanized. In some patients, ultra- sound may be more informative than endoscopy. 154 Postoperative Stomach Companion animals undergoing gastric surgery can have changes on postoperative imaging studies that mimic disease. It is often crucial when evaluating an imaging study to be familiar with the anatomic and physiologic changes that occur post- operatively as well as to be familiar with appropriate surgical techniques. One of the most common reasons for imaging the abdomen postoperatively include the evaluation of placed feeding tubes (gastric, gastrojejunal, etc.) or if the patient is not improving post gastric surgery as anticipated. Imaging proced- ures postoperatively can also be used to de ﬁ ne a baseline appearance, allowing detection of early or late postoperative complications. Radiography is often used as an initial technique to assess the extent of ﬂ uid and gas in the peritoneal cavity, position of the stomach, and presence and con ﬁ guration of surgical clips, staples, drains, and tubes. Postoperative functional disturbances of motility of the stomach and intestinal tract, paralytic ileus, and vomiting are not uncommon. If a subtotal gastrectomy is performed, no displacement of the stomach or stricture may be noted. 155 Similarly, if surgical gastric biopsies were performed, no displacement of the stomach would be expected. If a gastropexy was performed, which is a common procedure in dogs to prohibit GDV in the future by internally, permanently ﬁ xating the stomach to the abdominal wall in a way that gastric function is not affected, it is expected that the pylorus will be in close proximity to the right lateroventral abdominal wall. Radiographically, a caudoventral displacement of the pyloric antrum caudal to the last rib might be noted. If metallic staples were used for the gastropexy, they should be intact and the pyloric antrum should be near the staple line. Riedesel A bdominal imaging can assist in making a de ﬁ nitive diagnosis or in deciding between medical or surgical treatment in patients with clinical signs that implicate involvement of the small bowel. However, imaging ﬁ ndings must be interpreted in context with the signalment and history, and results from a thorough physical examination, and perti- nent laboratory tests. Survey radiographs and ultrasound eval- uation have become the primary imaging modalities for assessment of the small intestinal tract and surrounding struc- tures. Intestinal contrast studies are very useful in select situa- tions. The role of advanced imaging d mainly computed tomography (CT) and contrast-enhanced ultrasound (CEUS) d in the diagnosis of intestinal disease is beginning to be under- stood. This chapter will focus on radiographic and ultrasono- graphic imaging interpretation of the small bowel and how CT and CEUS are being used diagnostically. THE NORM AL SMAL L BOWEL Radiography Three-view abdominal radiography including both right lateral and left lateral in addition to the ventrodorsal (VD) view is the new standard for survey abdominal radiography and is dis- cussed in Chapter 38 1 The major rationale for the routine acquisition of all three views is to take advantage of the redis- tribution of intraluminal gas, leading to a more complete ex- amination. In the left lateral view, gastric gas, if present, can redistribute to the pyloric region, and usually also enter the duodenum and possibly the jejunum. If the VD is acquired after the left lateral view, gas will likely remain in the duodenum. Gas is more likely to be present in the duodenum in both the left lateral and VD views when the order of image acquisition is left lateral followed by VD followed by right lateral. 2 Other pro- cedures, such as compression radiographs, may also be useful in the assessment of the intestinal tract 3 ( Fig. 46.1 ). 1204: ( Fig. 46.4 ). In most instances, true thickening of the intestinal wall is better judged by ultrasound, contrast study, or palpation. The small bowel has ﬁ xed and moveable segments. In the dog, the cranial duodenal ﬂ exure is ﬁ xed along the caudal surface of the right side of the liver by the hepatoduodenal ligament. The descending duodenum lies along the right abdominal wall. The caudal duodenal ﬂ exure is located at a transverse plane through the tuber coxae with the ascending duodenum continuing cranially from this point on the left side of the root of the mesentery. The initial portion of the ascending duodenum is attached by the duodenocolic ligament. The jejunum should be distributed uniformly throughout the peritoneal cavity, occupying space not taken up by distensible organs (stomach or urinary bladder), solid organs (liver, spleen, or kidneys), or fat. The ileum crosses from the left to the right midabdomen to terminate at the ileocolic junction. The cat differs from the dog in the position of the cranial duodenal ﬂ exure. In the cat, the cranial ﬂ exure usually creates a sharper angle with the pylorus and is located closer to the midline. The descending duodenum courses in a gently curved loop, positioning the caudal duodenal ﬂ exure at approximately midabdomen. The position of the remainder of the small bowel is the same as the dog. Common positional variations of small bowel seen in normal dogs and cats include (1) a full stomach displacing the bowel caudally; (2) a distended urinary bladder displacing the bowel cranially; (3) intraperitoneal fat in obese cats causing the small bowel to be located centrally and/or on the right side; (4) in very obese cats, fat displacing the bowel into the central region of the abdominal cavity; and (5) in obese dogs, the bowel occupying the ventral portion of the pendulous abdominal cavity. Positional changes in the small intestine may also be indicative of disease in adjacent organs. The normal small bowel appears in survey radiographs as smooth, continuously curving tubes or as solid end-on circles or rings (see Fig. 46.1 ). Bowel shape is dependent on the projec- tion angle of the x-ray beam relative to the long or short axes of the loops and to the contractile activity of the smooth muscle. Segmental contractions give rise to spherical shapes; this is often described as string-of-pearls appearance in cats. Peri- staltic contractions cause long tubular shapes. 1205: The radiopacity of the normal small intestine is variable because of differing opacities of material within the lumen. In a nonfasted animal, any of the following may be seen in the lumen: gas, grainy-appearing mottled ingesta, which may include mineral (dirt, sand, bone) or metal, or ﬂ uid of homo- geneous soft tissue opacity. The nondiscretionary eating habits or diet type of some dogs and cats may result in mineral or metallic opacities of small size being present in the small bowel. Clay-based cat litter and small gravel from dog runs are common examples. Gastrointestinal medications that contain calcium, magnesium, aluminum, bismuth, or silicate can impart signi ﬁ cant radiopacity to the intestinal content. 9 Some pet vitamin and mineral supplements contain suf ﬁ cient mineral to be visible radiographically. In general, tablets or capsules containing minerals are more likely to be visible than liquids containing these minerals. 9 In a fasted animal, the lumen may contain a small amount of ingested air, or it may be of homogeneous ﬂ uid, or soft tissue opacity if it is collapsed. The amount of bowel that contains gas in the normal cat and dog is variable. Cats without gastrointestinal disease that are not fasted before radiography may have gas throughout the bowel. 7 In the fasted cat, gas is rarely present in the small intestine, but in fasted dogs, 30% to 60% of the small bowel content may be gas. 6 10 Animals stressed by handling or dyspneic animals frequently have a large amount of air in the small intestine due to aerophagia. The gas pattern is variable although most cats and dogs have a tubular pattern with gas in a continuous col- umn except where interrupted by contraction. The bowel wall should be of uniform soft tissue opacity. This uniformity is most easily assessed in segments that contain air. There are many small intestinal diseases that result in no survey radiographic changes. Regardless, survey radiographs are a valuable baseline prior to additional imaging studies such as ultrasound or contrast radiography. Some indications for these procedures are:  Acute, persistent vomiting with negative ﬁ ndings on sur- vey radiographs  Recurrent vomiting, especially in animals refractory to symptomatic therapy and without other organ disease to explain the vomiting  Palpable abdominal mass without obstructive bowel signs on survey radiographs  Acute abdominal pain with an unusual or unexplained ab- normality seen in the survey radiographs  Weight loss with intermittent or recurrent diarrhea  Melena or hematemesis Ultrasound The American College of Veterinary Radiology has provided a consensus statement on recommendations for performing an ultrasound examination of the gastrointestinal tract. 11 Obser- vations that can be made from intestinal ultrasonography include assessment of wall thickness, wall layer pattern, type of content, and motility. Transducer frequencies of 7.5 MHz and higher enable the best identi ﬁ cation of individual layers of the intestinal wall. Ultrasound imaging also allows assessment of structures adjacent to the intestine. The character of the mes- entery and regional lymph nodes and presence of abdominal ﬂ uid should be assessed. Evaluation of the small bowel should be part of a complete systematic evaluation including solid or- gans, particularly the pancreas and liver, and the gallbladder and common bile duct. Ultrasound-guided ﬁ ne-needle aspira- tion sampling for cytology and culture evaluation is useful in many patients. The major obstacle for optimal ultrasound imaging is the presence of gas in the bowel. The current recommendation is an 8- to 12-hour fast when the focus of the examination is the gastrointestinal tract in nonurgent patients. When gas is pre- sent, the far wall cannot be assessed. Repositioning the patient, using gravity-based transducer placement, or repeating the ex- amination later may overcome the artifacts induced by gas. Each intestinal segment should be examined in the longitu- dinal and transverse plane ( Fig. 46.6 ). 11 As many representative segments as possible of the jejunum and the ileocecocolic junction should be included. Both still and when possible, video clips of representative segments should be documented in the examination. The normal small intestinal wall consists of alternating hyperechoic and hypoechoic layers. When no ﬂ uid or gas is present, a thin, hyperechoic line represents the lumen. From the lumen to the serosa, the tissue layers and echogenicities are as follows: hypoechoic mucosa, hyperechoic submucosa, hypoechoic muscularis, and hyperechoic serosa (see Fig. 46.6 ). The hypoechoic mucosal layer is the thickest of the individual layers and thus is dominant visually. 12 When ﬂ uid is in the lumen, the mucosal surface is normally hyperechoic ( eFig. 46.1 ). If gas is in the lumen, a prominent ring-down reverberation artifact occurs as a stationary artifact in a rela- tively long length of bowel and as a moving reverberation artifact in peristaltic contraction. This artifact inhibits the assessment of the deeper wall. However, the presence of gas helps to identify the lumen in some abnormal segments. Lastly, all segments had a hyperechoic thin line in the muscularis layer that paral- leled the submucosal and serosal layers. Histologically, this was correlated with ﬁ brous tissue in the myenteric plexus located between the inner circular and outer longitudinal components of the muscularis propria. In most such patients, insuf ﬁ cient additional information will be gained because of the slow passage of contrast medium through atonic bowel proximal to the obstruction, especially in a weakened or debilitated animal, and the contrast study may delay or complicate a surgical procedure. If the clinical and survey radiographic ﬁ ndings are strongly suggestive of mechanical obstruction, an exploratory laparotomy can be justi ﬁ ed. Contrast studies are also not indicated in patients with sur- vey radiographic evidence of free peritoneal gas that is not re- sidual from recent laparotomy, penetrating trauma, or abdominocentesis as the gas is most likely from gastrointestinal perforation. 33 The combination of barium and intestinal con- tents within the peritoneal cavity causes more severe perito- nitis, foreign body granulomas, or serosal adhesions. 34 However, if treated promptly and aggressively, patient outcome can be good. 35 Attempting to identify the location of the perforation is not as important as providing aggressive medical and surgical intervention. Ultrasound can also be used to detect free peritoneal gas associated with gastrointestinal perforation and prevents the additional contamination associated with barium leakage. Water-soluble organic iodine contrast media are either ionic or nonionic. 36 Ionic iodinated contrast media are not recommended for oral administration in young and debilitated patients and especially dehydrated patients, because the resultant ﬂ uid shift can worsen any hypovolemic state. 37 Dual contrast radiography and ultrasonography can also be performed to assess the small intestine and is reported in healthy dogs. 38 Carboxymethylcellulose (0.5% solution) com- bined with iohexol (300 mg I/mL) and a dosage of 8.5 mL of carboxymethylcellulose/kg body weight and 1.5 mL of iohexol/ kg body weight as a mixture can be used to assess the small intestine both radiographically and ultrasonographically. The dual contrast medium served to improve the ultrasonographic assessment of the small intestine by mitigating reverberation artifact from intraluminal gas. Technique and General Interpretation A brief description of the techniques and interpretation of in- testinal contrast studies follows. More detailed descriptions are available elsewhere and discussed in Chapter 45 39 Contrast studies can be divided into two categories based on the radio- graphic opacity imparted by the contrast medium. Positive- contrast studies increase the opacity of the bowel lumen and are done with barium sulfate suspensions or iodinated prod- ucts. These contrast media are given orally or by orogastric intubation. Because the stomach is also opaci ﬁ ed by these agents, the phrase upper gastrointestinal contrast study is used. The volume of contrast medium in the intestinal lumen is critical for accurate interpretation. The intestine should be distended to its reasonable physiologic maximum. Failure to administer an adequate volume of contrast medium is one of the most frequent causes for a nondiagnostic barium study. Some recommended dosages for contrast medium are given in Table 46.4 . A summary of the portions of the gastrointestinal tract seen at speci ﬁ c intervals after positive-contrast medium administration is presented in Table 46.5 and in Chapter 45 Normal anatomic features of the duodenum made visible by positive-contrast medium should not be misinterpreted as le- sions. Dogs often have multiple square-shaped outpocketings on the antimesenteric side of the descending duodenum. One or several may be present. These are termed pseudoulcers and are normal and caused by mucosal depressions over submu- cosal lymphoid accumulations (see Fig. 46.5B ). Pseudoulcers are not found in the cat. Approximately 30% of normal cats have strong segmental contractions throughout the length of the duodenum that produce a string-of-pearls effect during the contrast study (see Fig. 46.5C ). 6 Throughout the remainder of the small bowel, concentric narrowing of short lengths of bowel should be seen and are caused by peristalsis ( eFig. 46.3 ). The location of such narrowing should vary during the time of study in the normal animal. In a normal upper gastrointestinal study, luminal barium and gas may be present simultaneously. A double-contrast effect is present when the distention by gas is greater than that caused by the barium. The barium/mucosa interface appears typically as a thin opaque line. In other segments, gas may be present only as small bubbles. Findings on the barium contrast images that most strongly correlate with abnormalities are changes in the diameter of the bowel, extensive changes in the barium/ mucosa interface, and changes in the rate of passage of barium. The intestinal tract is normally characterized by dynamic changes; thus, documenting a suspicious ﬁ nding on multiple radiographs over time increases the signi ﬁ cance of the ﬁ nding. Ileus can be mechanical, caused by physical obstruction of the bowel, or functional (paralytic), in which peristaltic contractions of the bowel cease because of vascular or neuromuscular abnormalities. In functional ileus, the bowel remains patent. The important imaging decision is whether the bowel dila- tion is indicative of a mechanical obstruction, and justi ﬁ es a laparotomy, or if additional diagnostic tests are needed. In all instances, imaging decisions should not be made in isolation of all other patient information. In general, the appearance of mechanically obstructed bowel differs from functionally obstructed bowel by the following parameters: 1. Mechanically obstructed bowel is usually of larger diam- eter than functionally obstructed bowel. 2. Patients with mechanical obstruction usually have a mixed population of dilated and normal-diameter bowel seg- ments, whereas patients with functional obstruction tend to have generalized mild dilation of the bowel. 3. Both gas and ﬂ uid are typically in the lumen of mechani- cally obstructed bowel, whereas functionally obstructed bowel tends to be completely gas ﬁ lled or contain general- ized ﬂ uid. These parameters, however, are only guidelines and some overlap exists between mechanical and functional ileus, making the radiographic distinction impossible in some patients. Mechanical Obstruction The small intestine can be occluded by foreign objects, intus- susception, mural mass, or extrinsic lesions. The radiographic features of small bowel obstruction depend on three factors: the completeness of the obstruction, the location of the obstruction in the gastrointestinal tract, and the duration. The most consistent radiographic sign of mechanical obstruction is a variable degree of dilation of bowel segments orad to the site of obstruction ( Fig. 46.16 eFig. 46.5 ). Subjective determination that bowel is signi ﬁ cantly dilated can be made accurately even by interpreters with a beginning level of interpretation expe- rience. 49 However, using ratios of small intestinal diameter to vertebral measurements may increase con ﬁ dence that obstructive bowel disease is present. In dogs, determining the ratio of the small intestinal diameter relative to the L5 vertebral body height can be used, but it must be remembered that this ratio is only a guideline. 5 A ratio less than 1.4 to 1.6 usually rules out mechanical obstruction. Ratios of 1.95 were associated with a 77% to 80% probability of obstruction and a ratio of 2.07 was associated with an 86% to 90% probability of obstruction (see Fig. 46.18 eFig. 46.6 ). 49 50 In a series of cats, when the maximum small intestinal diameter to L2 vertebral endplate height was > 2.0, gastrointestinal disease was present, and at a ratio of > 2.5, the most likely abnormality was intestinal obstruction. 7 A more distal obstruction leads to a greater number of dis- tended segments. Obstructed bowel typically contains both ﬂ uid and gas unless the obstruction is quite proximal, allowing gas and ﬂ uid to re ﬂ ux into the stomach. Depending on the location of a complete obstruction, there may be two distinctly different sizes of bowel with the smaller and normal diameter bowel distal or aboral to the dilated bowel. More complete and longer duration obstruction results in greater bowel distention. Acute duodenal obstruction is challenging to diagnose because the stomach acts as a reservoir for gas and ﬂ uid that might collect. Also, if vomiting is frequent, the accumulated ﬂ uid and gas are expelled from the stomach and duodenum. With chronic duodenal obstruction, however, gastric distention develops ( Fig. 46.18 ) and can be pronounced. A moderate to large volume of ﬂ uid and gas in the stomach, with an otherwise empty small intestinal tract, in a vomiting patient should raise suspicion of duodenal obstruction or pyloric out ﬂ ow obstruction. Partial obstructions may also be dif ﬁ cult to detect. This is particularly true when the partial obstruction is of short dura- tion and in the proximal duodenum. Longstanding partial distal obstructions result in accumulation of opaque granular material proximal to the site of obstruction. This is caused by desicca- tion of ingesta that becomes trapped proximal to the obstruc- tion. The desiccated material often has the appearance of feces, and the identi ﬁ cation of this fecal-like material in the small rather than large bowel is a reliable sign of partial distal small bowel obstruction. This appearance has been referred to as the gravel sign . One scenario in which chronic partial obstruction occurs is elderly cats that develop an ileal adenocarcinoma causing partial bowel obstruction ( Fig. 46.19 eFig. 46.7 ). Although sand particles are small, it is proposed that the sand coalesces and dehydrates to form the obstruction. Sequential radiographs can be used to monitor progression of the sand but if no progress is observed, a laparotomy should be considered. 53 A pneumocolon can be used to differentiate the source of dilated bowel as small intestine versus colon and can assist in de ﬁ ning the location of obvious foreign material or mottled mineralized material to be in the small versus large bowel ( Fig. 46.22 eFig. 46.11 ). The use of 24-hour serial survey ra- diographs, ultrasound evaluation, or a contrast study may be necessary to con ﬁ rm the diagnosis of partial obstruction sug- gested by abnormal luminal contents. Persistence of small opaque foreign objects in the same intestinal location in serial radiographs over a 24- to 48-hour period should increase the suspicion of partial obstruction. Two recent studies looked at the use of serial radiographs relative to mechanical bowel obstruction. One assessed the diagnostic accuracy of mechanical obstruction between initial and one follow-up radiograph between 7 and 28 hours. These dogs and cats ultimately had nonopaque foreign bodies causing partial or complete obstruction. Accuracy did not signi ﬁ cantly increase after the follow-up radiograph, and when the repeat radiograph is inclusive, alternate diagnostic studies such as ul- trasound should be considered. 54 The second study evaluated the incidence of resolution of mechanical obstruction and res- olution of gastrointestinal foreign bodies as assessed by repeat radiographs after 36-hour intervals of medical management. Approximately 17% of patients with only small intestine affected and 11% of patients with gastric plus small intestinal foreign bodies and mechanical obstruction resolved after medical management. 55 The ultrasonographic appearance of ingested foreign mate- rial varies according to the composition of the material ( Fig. 46.23 ). 56 The acoustic pattern caused by the rigid foreign object may have a shape that can be recognized speci ﬁ cally. Objects that transmit the beam, such as some types of rubber balls, are more readily identi ﬁ ed. Those that create a strong re ﬂ ection with marked acoustic shadowing can be more dif ﬁ cult to de ﬁ ne initially. When these objects cause incomplete obstruction, they are frequently associated with increased in- testinal motility resulting from irritation. With more complete obstruction, the foreign object may be associated with accu- mulation of ﬂ uid in the bowel cranial to the obstruction. In vomiting dogs, ultrasound ﬁ ndings of a jejunal serosa-to-serosa measurement of more than 1.5 cm, with normal wall layering, and a ﬂ uid- ﬁ lled or gas- ﬁ lled lumen should prompt careful interrogation of the bowel for an obstructive lesion. 57 A wide range of motility, from reduced to increased, was observed in dogs with mechanical obstruction and was not found to be a useful discriminatory feature relative to nonobstructive causes of vomiting. 57 Both dogs and cats can ingest linear foreign material. The mass form, found in 75% of cats with alimentary lymphoma, is expressed as transmural circumferential thickening in the transverse plane (4 22 mm) with the wall layers replaced by hypoechoic or mixed echo- genicity tissue and is due to high-grade alimentary lymphoma (HGAL) of small or large lymphocytes of B- or T-cell type ( Fig. 46.35 ). About half of cats have associated enlargement of the mesenteric lymph nodes. 109 110 The second pattern is that of LGITL that has preserved wall layers but exhibits thickening of the muscular layer Fig. 46.33 There are bulges de forming the contour of a focal segment ofsmall bowel. Ultrasound wall layering changes have been documented in cats with both LGITL and in ﬂ ammatory enter- opathy to differentiate from healthy individuals. 111 Thickening of the muscular layer in the cat has been attributed to compensatory hypertrophy in response to a distal obstruction and idiopathic hypertrophy in the absence of obstruction. 112 113 The idiopathic form has also been associated with chronic enteritis. 113 The thickness of the muscularis of the duodenal and jejunal segments of 14 cats with small cell T-cell lymphoma and IBD and 19 healthy cats was compared. Increased (two times as thick) thickness of the muscularis propria was found in both affected groups compared to healthy cats. 109 Colic lymph nodes in this population in cats with lymphoma were increased compared to healthy cats. These ﬁ ndings are similar to that in a study of 300 cats with full- thickness biopsy con ﬁ rmed in ﬂ ammatory enteropathy (150 cats) or LGITL (124) and it was determined that the two etiol- ogies cannot be differentiated based on wall layering and thickness. 110 In this study, it was also established that 86% of cats with a total wall thickness 2.8 mm had in ﬁ ltrative disease of one or the other etiologies and suggested that segmental thickening could indicate more diffuse disease. Fewer sonographic characteristics have been described for speci ﬁ c intestinal neoplasms in the dog. Differentiation of leiomyosarcoma from leiomyoma has been proposed based on leiomyosarcoma being larger (2 8 cm thick), eccentric, and having mixed echogenicity. 107 However, these patients were evaluated prior to the reclassi ﬁ cation of many smooth muscle intestinal tumors as GISTs. In a more recent comparison of GIST and spindle cell tumors of the gastrointestinal tract, there were no speci ﬁ c ultrasound features that were distinguishing. Biopsy with immunohistochemical staining was needed to differentiate these tumors. The larger a bowel mass becomes, the more likely it is to have necrosis, which will appear as intralesional hypoechoic foci. Tumors that enlarge by exophytic growth can become quite large before clinical signs develop since they do not narrow the intestinal lumen. Other tumors of the canine small intestine are reported insuf ﬁ ciently to enable any con- clusions about trends in their sonographic appearance ( Fig. 46.37 ). Ultrasound evaluation of the intestine combined with ultrasound-guided ﬁ ne-needle aspiration and microcore biopsy is an accurate method of minimally invasive diagnosis ( Fig. 46.38 ). 109 However, depending on the sampling site, different outcomes in the same animal with both in ﬂ ammatory and neoplastic in ﬁ ltrative disease are possible. 30 Metastatic bowel tumors are uncommon. Metastasis of mammary carcinoma to the jejunal muscular layer has been identi ﬁ ed in a dog, and appeared as focal hypoechoic nodules. 114 Infectious enteritis may be caused by viruses, bacterial, rickettsial, fungal (and fungal-like), or more rarely parasitic or- ganisms ( Fig. 46.39 ). Changes associated with parvovirus (canine parvovirus type 2) have been discussed earlier regarding abnormal bowel dilation. If parvoviral enteritis is suspected, imaging should be delayed until clinical testing can be performed. Other viral diseases that infect the small intesti- nal tract do not cause any speci ﬁ c radiographic or sonographic changes and thus are not discussed here. Bacterial overgrowth in the small intestine has also not been related to speci ﬁ c radiographic or sonographic changes. Heterobilharzia americana (HA) or canine schistosomiasis can cause infection of the small intestines in addition to affecting other body organs. 115 Pathologically the trematode in ﬁ ltrates the submucosa with oocytes and causes a granulo- matous response. Radiographically, dogs with chronic enter- opathy can show mineralization of the small intestinal wall. The mineralization is not consistently associated with hypercalce- mia. In one report the mineralization was associated with a large number of calci ﬁ ed eggs in the bowel and other organs. 116 Ultrasonographically, the submucosa can be recognized as ill- de ﬁ ned thickening or contain variable degrees of pinpoint hyperechoic foci. 117 119 Hyperechoic foci can also be seen in the liver and mesenteric lymph nodes. In an assessment of HA- positive dogs compared to control dogs, thickening of the submucosa layer concurrent with the presence of hyperechoic foci in the liver, small intestine, and mesenteric lymph nodes provided differentiation of the infected dogs. The endemic range of HA is along the Atlantic and Gulf Coast of North America. Canine cases have also been diagnosed in Kansas, Oklahoma, Arkansas, Indiana, and Utah 120 122 ( Fig. 46.40 ). In both the canine and the feline patient, IBD refers to a group of disorders of unde- termined etiology that cause chronic ( > 3 weeks) vomiting and/ or diarrhea and have various populations of in ﬂ ammatory cells in the bowel wall layers. 123 125 The most common of these is a lymphocytic-plasmacytic enteritis. Some breed-associated forms of IBD have been described d immunoproliferative enteropathy of Basenjis, familial protein-losing enteropathy (PLE) and protein-losing nephropathy in soft-coated Wheaten terriers, and gluten-sensitive enteropathy in Irish setters. 123 None of these breed-speci ﬁ c disorders have unique radiographic or ultraso- nographic diagnostic ﬁ ndings. Equivocal radiographic and sonographic ﬁ ndings suggest additional diagnostic tests are necessary. In ﬂ ammatory in ﬁ ltrates are expected to increase bowel wall thickness or alter the character of the tissue. However, bowel wall thickness cannot be used to differentiate normal from affected dogs, although some dogs have mild thickening. 123 126 The ﬁ nding of normal wall thickness may lead to a signi ﬁ cant rate of false-negative diagnoses in animals with in ﬂ ammatory in ﬁ ltrates ( Fig. 46.41 ). Distinction of PLE from IBD and food-responsive disease in dogs is based on ﬁ nding increased mucosal layer echogenicity with PLE, because of varying severity of hyperechoic vertical striations in the duodenum and jejunum ( Fig. 46.42 ). Histolog- ically, the vertical striations are associated with lym- phangiectasia. 124 127 128 Dogs with IBD and food-responsive disease can also have increased echogenicity in the mucosal layer described as hyperechoic speckles, being oriented in a horizontal or focal dot pattern compared to the striation pattern. Total bowel wall thickening is inconsistent in PLE and, when present, is mild. Secondary ﬁ ndings in dogs with PLE included peritoneal effusion, edema of the pancreas, and distended bowel segments; however, these ﬁ ndings can also be present in dogs with IBD. Dogs with food-responsive disease do not typically have these secondary ﬁ ndings. Intestinal biopsy remains the de ﬁ nitive diagnostic test for in ﬁ ltrative bowel disease. Focal lipogranulomatous lymphangitis is a rare and severe form of canine IBD. 129 130 The etiology is undetermined, and diagnosis is made by histopathologic changes. Of the 17 dogs reported, most lesions occurred in the distal ileum and had sonographic changes of thickened wall (6 14 mm), retained layers, but with predominantly thickened muscular layer. Regional lymph nodes were enlarged but of normal echoge- nicity. Three dogs had an associated mass up to 4 cm in size extending from the serosa or in the adjacent mesentery. In ﬂ ammation, ﬁ brosis, and necrosis mixed with dilated lacteals and lymphatic vessels are identi ﬁ ed at histopathology. Bowel-Associated Masses Bowel-associated masses can be due to abscesses, hematomas, fungal granulomas, eosinophilic in ﬂ ammation, and neoplasms. Bacterial abscesses can occur as focal lesions associated with the intestinal wall. A bowel-associated abscess can be a conse- quence of partial or complete intestinal perforation by foreign material with subsequent adhesions and abscess formation. The mass may result in regional loss of serosal detail or may displace adjacent bowel ( Fig. 46.43 ). A mottled appearance may be seen in bowel-associated abscesses when exudate from the abscess drains into the lumen and is replaced by gas (see Fig. 46.43 ). Abscesses associated with the small intestine may originate from a source extrinsic to the wall. This may occur because of retained surgical sponges (gossypiboma) or be caused by a pancreatic abscess. Small intestinal wall hematoma has been reported with intestinal wire foreign body perforation. 131 Although uncommon, mycotic infections of the intestinal tract include histoplasmosis, cryptococcosis, 132 and pythiosis. Diffuse miner- alization of the wall can occur by metastatic calci ﬁ cation because of hypercalcemia. Dogs and cats poisoned by cholecalciferol-based rodenticides and having ingested human antipsoriasis ointment containing calcitriol analogues can develop vomiting, which may lead to radiography and/or ul- trasonography of the abdomen. 139 142 Diffuse calci ﬁ cation of the gastrointestinal tract may be found in these patients. Radiographically, the degree of calci ﬁ cation typically creates a thin line of opacity, imparting an enhanced contrast effect. Differential diagnosis for this type of diffuse mineralization should include other causes of hypercalcemia, including severe primary renal disease. 1244: Christine L. Gremillion ANAT OMY The large intestine consists of the cecum, colon, rectum, and anal canal ( Fig. 47.1 ). The cecum is a diverticulum arising from the proximal colon, located in the right midabdomen, at approximately the level of L3 and L4. 1 The cecum can be quite variable in shape and size depending on its luminal contents. In dogs, the cecum tends to be larger and sigmoid or c-shaped, whereas in cats the cecum is shorter in length and more cone- shaped ( Fig. 47.2 ). 1 2 The mesentery of the colon (mesocolon) is present along its entire length, and is shorter than the mes- entery of the small intestine. The mesocolon is also attached to the mesoduodenum via the duodenocolic ligament. These fac- tors combine to make the large intestine overall less mobile than the small intestine, and thus, its normal position within the abdomen is more consistent. 1 The colon is divided into three parts: the ascending, transverse, and descending colon. The ascending colon is the most proximal portion of the colon, located in the cranial abdomen to the right of midline. The ascending colon is located near the descending duodenum, right lobe of the pancreas, and right kidney. The right colic ﬂ exure connects the ascending colon to the transverse colon. The transverse colon lives in the cranial abdomen, coursing from the right to left side, and is located adjacent to the greater curvature of the stomach and left lobe of the pancreas. The transverse colon communicates with the descending colon at the left colic ﬂ exure. The descending colon then courses caudally, parallel to the body wall, to the level of the pelvic inlet, where it transitions into the rectum without demarcation. The terminal portion of the descending colon and rectum are located dorsal to the urinary bladder, urethra, and prostate/ uterus. The rectum then continues caudally to the level of the second or third caudal vertebrae, where it communicates with the anal canal. 1 IMAG ING PROC EDUR ES Radiography Normal Radiographic Findings The colon is often readily visible on plain radiographs due to normal intraluminal gas and/or fecal contents, although areas devoid of contents may be indistinct. Fecal material often has a granular appearance with mixed soft tissue and gas opacity. The normal colon is shaped like a question mark or shepherd s crook, coursing from the ileocolic junction in the right mid- abdomen cranially, across midline, and then caudally along the left abdomen in the ventrodorsal view. Contrast Radiography Contrast radiography of the large intestine may be utilized when the diagnosis or appropriate treatment for a patient cannot be determined by survey radiographs and other imaging modalities are not available or desirable. The use of ultrasound and direct inspection of the large intestine via endoscopy have largely replaced many radiographic contrast studies of the co- lon 2 ; however, contrast studies are still helpful for speci ﬁ c indications. Pneumocolonography Pneumocolonography, or negative contrast studies of the co- lon, are typically performed in patients to determine the posi- tion of the colon on radiographs and to differentiate it from distended small intestines. 3 6 Pneumocolonography has also been described in aiding the diagnosis of colonic torsion. 7 Survey radiographs should always be acquired ﬁ rst. With the patient positioned in lateral recumbency, approximately 1 to 3 mL/kg of air is introduced into a red-rubber catheter that is placed in the rectum and then lateral and ventrodorsal pro- jections are obtained. 6 The ﬁ nal volume of air required to suf- ﬁ ciently ﬁ ll the entirety of the colon is patient dependent, and often small increments of air are introduced, radiographs are acquired, and if there is an insuf ﬁ cient volume, the process is repeated. In most patients, it is desirable to ﬁ ll the entirety of the colon with air to the level of the cecum. Survey radiographs should always be obtained prior to initiation of the study. Unless performed as an emergency procedure, preparation including a 12- to 24-hour fast, laxa- tives, and cleansing enemas is preferred. 9 The volume of contrast medium utilized depends on the indication for the study. A dose of approximately 10 to 15 mL/kg of body weight of barium suspension can be expected to ﬁ ll the entirety of the colon 3 9 ; however, this full volume is not required for diagnosis of all disease processes. A diagnosis of colonic torsion has been made using dosages of as little as 3 mL/kg of body weight. 10 Barium is usually administered via an in ﬂ atable Foley catheter placed in the distal rectum. 4 8 9 To minimize risk of perforation, the colon should either be ﬁ lled slowly by gravity or infused in small increments until the desired effect is seen radiographi- cally. Both lateral and ventrodorsal projections should be ac- quired following introduction of barium. If back pressure is present on the syringe, infusion of barium should be dis- continued. If colonic perforation is suspected prior to initiation of the study, iodinated contrast medium should be used instead of barium due to the risk of granulomatous peritonitis with extravasation of barium. 9 Ultrasound of the Large Bowel Ultrasound allows assessment of large intestinal wall thickness, layering, and evidence of mass lesions, and also provides the ability to assess the surrounding mesentery and regional lymph nodes. Ultrasound-guided tissue sampling ( ﬁ ne needle aspirate or biopsy) can also be performed. 11 The primary limitation of ultrasound of the large bowel is the presence of feces and gas with distal acoustic shadowing and reverberation artifacts, respectively, which result in limited visibility of the bowel wall in the far- ﬁ eld of the image. The wall of the large intestine is thinner than that of the small intestine, measuring only 1 to 2 mm in thickness on ul- trasound. 12 Similar to the stomach and small intestine, distinct wall layers of the large intestine are visible: a hyperechoic luminal surface, hypoechoic mucosa, hyperechoic submucosa, hypoechoic muscularis, and hyperechoic outer serosa ( Fig. 47.5 ). When the colon is empty, the wall can have an irregular appearance due to infolding and should not be confused with wall thickening. Occasionally, a thin hyper- echoic line can be seen in the muscularis layer of the colon that parallels the serosal surface. Histologically, this correlates with ﬁ brous tissue in the myenteric plexus. As this is seen in dogs without a history of diarrhea, this ﬁ nding is considered a normal variant. 13 The descending colon can be easily recognized when imaging in a transverse plane in the caudal abdomen, where it lies dorsal to the urinary bladder at the pelvic inlet. The typical appearance of the colon is a thin-walled tubular structure with a curved hyperechoic luminal interface. When identi ﬁ ed near the urinary bladder, the descending colon can then be traced cranially through the remainder of the large bowel. The ileo- colic junction ( Fig. 47.6 ), cecum, and ascending colon are located medial to the right kidney, which can serve as a land- mark as well if unable to trace the entirety of the colon from distal to proximal. Computed Tomography of the Large Bowel Computed tomography (CT) provides a three-dimensional view of the large bowel and surrounding structures and is particu- larly helpful for assessing abnormalities within the pelvic canal compared to radiographs and ultrasound ( Fig. 47.7 ). 14 When nonionic iodinated contrast medium is administered intrave- nously, the colonic mucosa strongly enhances, but discrete wall layers are not visible on CT. 15 Water, barium, and air have been described as luminal contrast agents. 16 17 Bowel preparation protocols may be utilized for bowel cleansing to optimize im- age quality and aid in interpretation. 18 LARGE BO WEL DISEAS ES Large Intestinal Displacement From Mass Effect Abnormalities of the organs adjacent to the large intestine can result in displacement, and sometimes compression, of the colon and rectum depending on the severity ( Figs. 47.8 and 47.9 ). Moderate to severe enlargement of the iliosacral lymph center will result in ventral displacement of the colon and/or rectum on lateral radiographs ( Fig. 47.10A ). Ventral displace- ment of the colon will also occur secondary to renomegaly and other causes of mass effects from the retroperitoneal space such as retroperitoneal effusion. 1251: Displacement From Herniation Perineal Hernia In addition to herniation of the bladder and/or prostate into the perineal region, perineal hernias also frequently result in displacement of the rectum and/or descending colon into the perineal region ( Fig. 47.17 ). Alterations in Large Bowel Diameter Constipation/Obstipation/Megacolon Constipation is de ﬁ ned as reversible, infrequent, or dif ﬁ cult defecation with associated retention of fecal material. 2 Recur- rent constipation that is refractory to treatment is termed obstipation , and implies a permanent loss of function. 2 Mega- colon is a descriptive term, used when there is irreversible dilation of the colon, and represents end-stage colonic dysfunction in patients with obstipation. 2 5 ( Fig. 47.18 ; eFig. 47.5A,B ) Differentials for patients with chronic constipation, obstipation, and megacolon can be split into functional and mechanical causes. Functional causes include neuromuscular dysfunction; spinal cord diseases, including lumbosacral, cauda equina, and sacral spinal cord deformities (such as that seen in the Manx cat); hypogastric or pelvic nerve disorders; submu- cosal or myenteric plexus neuropathy; aganglionosis of the large bowel; and feline dysautonomia. 2 30 32 Metabolic and endocrine diseases can also be a functional cause of chronic constipation, with young cats with congenital hypothyroidism being particularly predisposed. 2 33 34 Mechanical causes of chronic constipation include luminal obstruction secondary to mural lesions of the large intestine (such as masses or stric- tures), h ern iat io n of la r ge bo we l w it h a s s oci a te d o bs tr uc ti on , an d co ng en it al d ef or mi ti e s s u ch a s at res ia ani a nd a tr es ia c ol i. MURAL ABN ORMALITI ES OF THE LARG E BOWEL Focal Wall Thickening Focal wall thickening and mass lesions of the large intestine occur secondary to in ﬁ ltration of the wall with cells, most commonly secondary to neoplasia, in ﬂ ammation, and/or infec- tious disease. Mass lesions of the large intestine may be visible on radiographs if they are large in size; small lesions are better visualized with ultrasound. Ultrasound ﬁ ndings include focal thickening of the intestinal wall and/or discrete nodules/masses arising from the intestinal wall with alteration or loss of wall layering. While neoplasia is a common cause of these changes, these ﬁ ndings are not speci ﬁ c and there is overlap between neoplastic and in ﬂ ammatory lesions. Patient signalment, his- tory, clinical signs, and lesion location can sometimes aid in prioritizing differential diagnoses, but ultimately, tissue sam- pling must be performed for de ﬁ nitive diagnosis. 1255: Focal Wall Thickening From Infectious/ In ﬂ ammatory Disease A variety of infectious and in ﬂ ammatory diseases can result in focal wall thickening or mass lesions of the large intestine with alteration or complete loss of wall layering. In dogs, conditions reported to cause focal masses with loss of wall layering of the colon include pythiosis, fungal disease, and protothecosis. 39 42 Granulomatous colitis can also cause focal wall thickening and masses. 43 Submucosal thickening and mineralization of the co- lon wall have been reported in dogs secondary to Hetero- bilharzia americana infection, although these changes are often less pronounced than that seen in the small intestine. 44 45 In cats, feline infectious peritonitis, fungal disease, and eosin- ophilic sclerosing ﬁ broplasia can result in mass lesions and focal thickening of the large intestine. 46 47 In both dogs and cats, bacterial etiologies, such as disseminated mycobacteriosis, can result in focal or multifocal intestinal lesions. 48 Benign Mass Lesions of the Large Intestine Benign polyps have been reported in the large intestine of both dogs and cats, and have rarely been associated with intussus- ception. 21 38 49 Adenomas and leiomyomas are benign neo- plasms that can occur within the large intestine, although these are less common than their malignant counterparts (adenocar- cinoma and leiomyosarcoma, respectively). Hemorrhage and/or hematoma formation within the wall can also result in focal mass lesions of the large bowel, 50 and cecal mucoceles are a cause of intraluminal mass-like lesions which could be confused for a soft tissue mass. 51 Diffuse Wall Thickening Colitis/Typhlitis With colitis, a gas- or ﬂ uid- ﬁ lled colon may be seen radio- graphically. On ultrasound, mild diffuse thickening of the wall may be present ( Fig. 47.22 ), usually with preservation of wall layers, in conjunction with echogenic intraluminal ﬂ uid.
